item.title: Mental health challenges in the AI safety ecosystem seem like a big problem
item.description:
Published on August 11, 2026 8:00 PM GMT

A tough lesson I learned over the past few years is that it’s pretty stressful to work in the “Please Don’t Build the Torment Nexus” ecosystem, especially as it increasingly seems like the world is hell-bent on building the Torment Nexus.

It’s hard to be productive when you’re stressed and anxious. And setting aside productivity, it’s also just plain bad if people working on AI safety — My peers! My people! — are feeling distraught.

Anxiety about AI risk really fucking sucks. If you feel this way, you aren’t alone. I’m right by your side, biting my nails, whitening my knuckles.

But even besides me, a lot of people seem to feel this way.

How big of a problem is this?

Survey data[1] described in Spencer Greenberg’s recent 80k episode implies that mental health challenges for people working on AI safety are fairly common:

Most respondents experienced psychological challenges — the median person reported six different problems.

More than half (52%) said these challenges at least moderately hurt their effectiveness, while 45% had considered cutting back or leaving.

The most common problems were:

  • Difficulty switching off from work: 68%
  • Imposter syndrome: 60%
  • Burnout: 59%
  • Guilt: 56%
  • Anxiety or worry: 54%

Less common — though still significant — were loneliness or isolation (32%), hopelessness or depression (29%), interpersonal difficulties (28%), and fear of death (22%).

Few appeared to be experiencing clinical anxiety or depressive disorders. The more typical problem was chronic strain: people remained functional, but struggled to rest, sustain motivation, and maintain boundaries.

Somewhat ironically, I asked Fable 5 to estimate BOTEC how much productivity is being lost due to mental health challenges in the AI safety ecosystem. It estimated a loss of roughly 6–7% of total workforce output, with an 80% confidence interval of ~3 to 13%. I only quickly skimmed the report it put together, but the conclusion seems fairly reasonable to me. If anything, my all-things-considered guess is that the real productivity hit is larger.

If I’m right, this seems like a big problem. And as a corollary, if tractable interventions exist here, even modest improvements would be worth a lot.[2]

What is being done about it?

There’s a bunch of existing stuff I’m aware of related to mental health and AI safety:

  • EA Mental Health Navigator and MentNav, which provide some mental health resources for effective altruists.
  • Rethink Wellbeing, which seems to run 8-week guided online programs, group-based peer support formats led by trained laypeople.
  • I’ve seen a bunch of surveys about mental health run over the years, e.g., this, this, and this (which I referenced above).
  • The EA forum has a topic on self-care and wellbeing.
    • There’s a ton of writing about mental health challenges related to AI safety on the EA Forum and LessWrong (this post in particular seems like a useful snapshot, though note it’s from 2023; also, see this).
  • Many people (myself included) like this 80k podcast episode. There’s also this one, which inspired this blog post.
    • Spencer talks about his book. I haven’t (yet) read it, but maybe it’s good!

What else should be done about it on the margin?

Honestly, I don’t know. I’m not sure how tractable this is, and I don’t claim to have particularly great ideas. With this post, I’m mostly just trying to point at a problem, say “oh man, this seems like a big problem”, and hope that others have ideas for how to fix it.[3]

That said, here are a few things that might be good:

  • A vetted network of therapists who “get it”. I think it would be good if there was a curated, actively maintained, network of clinicians who have experience working with AI safety clients. As mentioned above, there’s the EA Mental Health Navigator — and ACX has the Psychiat-List — but maybe more can be done? When I was searching for a therapist, I didn’t find these existing resources super helpful.
  • Better norms in the community. The survey implies that chronic strain (e.g., issues with boundaries, rest, and motivation) is more common than clinical disorders like anxiety or depression. So maybe a lot of the fix has to do with improving the norms that shape the day-to-day experience of working on AI safety. For instance, not socially rewarding hardcoreness as a virtue so strongly.
  • Expand the group-program model. Rethink Wellbeing’s peer-guided CBT/IFS groups seem useful, at first glance. Maybe someone could do an AI-safety-specific version?
  • Generous mental health benefits at AI safety orgs. My sense is that many AI safety orgs are good at providing mental health benefits for their employees, but I might be wrong. If the org you run doesn’t offer this, you probably should fix that.
  • Peer support circles. Lightly facilitated, informal-ish groups of people working on AI safety who meet on some regular cadence to support each other emotionally.
  • Manager upskilling. Maybe someone (a high-AI-safety-context therapist?) could create resources or offer training sessions on how managers can provide better support to their direct reports.

If you’re interested in starting a project on something like this (or something else aimed at improving mental health in the AI safety space), this RFP from Coefficient Giving might be a good place to get funding. You also might want to check out the EA infrastructure fund.

If you’re applying for funding for some other project/org, consider requesting additional funding specifically to support yourself/your employees with mental health related challenges.

  1. ^

    The survey is of 80 people working on existential risk, AI safety, animal welfare, and other high-impact causes. There’s obviously some self-selection bias here, but even after accounting for that, the rates of mental health challenges seem quite high to me. And while the survey population is broader than AI safety specifically, I'm assuming the AI safety subset looks similar (if anything, plausibly worse), but I haven't checked.

  2. ^

    The AI safety ecosystem has a high willingness-to-pay for interventions that bring new people into the field. In theory, the willingness-to-pay for interventions that help AI safety people who are struggling with mental health challenges (and are thus less productive than they otherwise could be) should also be high.

    After doing some fake math, I'd guess that the ecosystem should be willing to pay at least millions of dollars (maybe tens of millions?!) for something that reduces the productivity drag by a percentage point.

  3. ^

    Ironically, one of the hallmarks of AI safety work is that problem diagnosis is enticingly easy, whereas solution generation is much harder.

item.title: Slot hiring vs bar hiring
item.description:
Published on August 12, 2026 11:45 AM GMT

This is from Same Page, a blog about EA-org-style management I write with Max Dalton of Forethought.

Defining slot vs. bar hiring

I’m fairly confident this distinction has been kicking around the effective altruism movement for at least eight years. I didn’t invent it, and I’m not sure who did. Claude and I couldn’t find a public write-up of the idea, so I’ve made one.

In slot hiring, an organisation decides it has a particular position to fill (or maybe two positions, or more). It runs a hiring round, picks the best candidate it finds, and makes an offer. If that person declines, it makes the offer to the next-best, and so on.

Most of the world operates in slot hiring, so it’s the model most people have internalised for how organisations work.

In bar hiring, an organisation defines a threshold of fit and hires anyone above it. The strength of the candidate pool determines how many offers are made.

Thoughts on how to think about slot vs. bar hiring

An organisation wants to hire up to the point where further recruitment stops being the most valuable use of its resources.

The choice between bar and slot hiring mostly comes down to whether we land on that point more reliably by (a) specifying how many hires to make ahead of time, or (b) asking hiring managers to make a judgement call on whether candidates meet a bar.

When to slot vs. bar hire

Here are some key factors which drive that decision:[1]

1. Is there a steep drop-off in how much value an additional hire can add?

If there’s some very valuable work which ‘must’ be done, but additional work is lower in value, then we’ll get a steeply diminishing returns curve.

For example, in a town of 1000 people, it’s very important to have at least one doctor so that we have someone who can treat the very highest ‘value per doctor time’ conditions (for example, heart attacks and appendicitis). It’s really important to have a second doctor, it’s ideal to have a third doctor, but the tenth doctor isn’t adding much and the 100th doctor adds a trivial amount.

This means that we should try extremely hard to have at least one doctor — and whether to hire is dominated by the number of existing doctors (rather than by their quality). Whereas in a city of a million, the difference in value added by the 1000th doctor is only very slightly less than the 1001st doctor.

When you’re building an organisation and looking to create roles which you can ‘bar hire’ for, you want to look for places where you expect the curve to be gradual rather than steep.

(I’ve written about this in proven talent profiles.)

2. Is there a steep drop-off in how strong your top candidates are?

A gradual drop-off favours slot hiring. You can figure out the ideal number of hires to make before you start hiring, because the decision about whether to make 1 or 3 hires isn’t very dependent on the specifics of who turns up.

I expect the best way to know the shape of your curve is with experience, or asking others who have experience.[2]

3. How effectively can your organisation execute on hiring staff at the bar?

Specifying a number of hires to meet is very legible. In contrast, specifying a bar is complicated and difficult for leadership to verify.

By using slot hiring, organisations are often guarding against principal-agent problems where staff take actions which benefit them rather than the organisation — for example if a manager wanted to hire a large team because it’d look good on their CV. Giving a manager a set number of slots rather than asking them to make a judgement call on the bar is one way to reduce these.[3]

But as leadership and hiring managers are more synced up, bar hiring becomes more possible. And, if you can make it easier to determine whether a staff member meets the bar (for example, by building a process around a set of proven talent profiles), you can increase how legible the bar is. That will make bar hiring more attractive.

Navigating the bar shifting up and down

Where the bar should sit moves up and down over time.

As above, this is because an organisation will want to hire up to the point where further recruitment stops being the most valuable use of its resources — and that point will be subject to many changes as strategy and the relative importance of bottlenecks shift over time.

For example, if a huge number of applicants suddenly turned up who all cleared the current bar, management capacity would get overwhelmed, onboarding systems would get overwhelmed, you’d run into a funding bottleneck, and so on.

Or consider an advocacy nonprofit, one which wants a fundraising function, a research function, and a content or marketing function. Its impact is roughly the product of their strength across these three areas.

If the marketing function is already strong and already covering the most valuable work, adding additional marketers will add much less value than improving either of the other two programmes.

But it can get worse than that. If we model a marginal marketer as drawing on some org resources which might otherwise be used to improve the other two programmes (for example, CEO attention, funding, recruiting team support), the cost of a marketer could reach or exceed the benefits.

In this case, marketing has moved into a steep drop-off scenario, and you should raise the bar until you’re only hiring marketers who are so strong that they add enough value to compensate for the opportunity costs.

(I think that the right way to think about this technically is as a production function. I’ve mused on that topic in contexts like 80k’s here.)

Always be hiring

A major advantage of being in bar mode is that it enables you to hire all the time. You can apply that bar to anyone who shows up and evaluate them against it — whether it’s through referrals, networks, side conversations between open rounds, or random messages.

This really is very useful! But it comes with a cost: every time a potential candidate comes on your radar, you need to make the tricky decision of whether to investigate them further.

That’s a genuinely hard and highly context-dependent question.

I have two potentially useful pointers:

  1. Think about it as a value-of-information question.
  2. See if you have any moves available to you which will allow you to make progress rapidly. My ideas are here.
  1. ^

    I’m still pretty sure I’m messing up the ontology somewhere. Every time I look at it my view shifts somewhat. If you figure out a clean overview, do let me know!

  2. ^

    Rob Wiblin worked this through theoretically in How replaceable are the top candidates in large hiring rounds?

  3. ^

    Setting up hiring committees with at least one member from another internal team is another way to help here, as the non-team member can add perspective on the org-wide hiring bar and might notice when the hiring team is biased in favour of making a hire that would be unwise for the org overall.

item.title: What 27 AI Safety Generalists Are Building This Summer
item.description:
Published on August 12, 2026 6:12 PM GMT

This summer, 27 residents came to Berkeley for the first cohort of the Generator Residency, a three-month program for AI safety generalists run by Kairos and Constellation.

Residents receive mentorship from experienced generalists and researchers and are working on projects like running workshops for professionals entering AI safety, building a cross-org talent directory, supporting university AI safety groups, serving as chiefs of staff at new and growing organizations, building tools for model welfare and model spec research, and more. See more about each of their projects below.

Lateral Workshop

Seth Lifland and Jacob Brinton

We're running Lateral Workshop, a fully funded three-day program helping experienced professionals explore transitions into AI safety. Many mid-career and senior professionals have skills the field urgently needs, including organizational leadership, government experience, cybersecurity, communications, law, finance, and operations. Yet entering AI safety can be difficult because the ecosystem is unfamiliar, professional networks are limited, and the financial and reputational risks of changing careers are substantial.

Held September 11–13 in Berkeley, Lateral Workshop will bring together promising professionals and people already working in AI safety through expert talks, small-group discussions, one-on-one conversations, and a community mixer. The program aims to make the field easier to understand, help participants identify where their existing experience could be most useful, connect them with organizations and potential collaborators, and introduce practical resources such as career-transition grants. Participants will also receive continued support after the workshop.

Learn more at lateralworkshop.org. Applications closed August 9th, but you can express interest in future workshops here. If you know someone who’d be a great fit, refer them here. You can reach out at contact@lateralworkshop.org.

Jeff Alstott’s Chief of Staff

Matt Handzel

I've been Jeff Alstott’s Chief of Staff for a new organization he is starting. I'm focusing the largest chunk of my time on recruiting: writing job descriptions, creating the hiring backend, and reaching out to potential candidates. I believe being Jeff's Chief of Staff is the best way I can gain experience in founding and scaling new organizations. I think this is a highly leveraged opportunity for impact.

Have a low bar to reach out!

Check out my personal website: https://www.matthandzel.com

Forward-deployed AI engineering for AI safety orgs

Matthew Kenney

I focused on object-level automation for model welfare research across three areas. First, I built a collaborative platform for conducting model welfare interviews and annotating self-reports. Researchers can run and branch conversations, leave notes, automate interviewer turns, and review AI-generated annotations using structured codebooks. The system is designed to automate repetitive elicitation and annotation work while keeping researchers in the loop for interpretation and approval.

I also developed structured welfare-relevant benchmarks covering self-report consistency, framing effects, model-family differences, and responses following different task conditions. Finally, I studied whether models can report decision policies learned through training. These experiments found that self-reports contain real information about learned policies and respond to causal changes, but are attenuated, prompt-sensitive. Together, this work helps identify which parts of model welfare research can be automated and where human validation and stronger measurement methods remain necessary.

Improving management in AI safety

Joe Hajj

My project focuses on making AI safety managers more effective, which is increasingly important as the field scales and more individual contributors become managers. Typically, new AIS managers don't get training when stepping into the role and commonly learn through trial and error, ad-hoc mentorship, or scrambling to find resources on their own. I interviewed 10+ AIS managers about the challenges they face, built a curriculum from the findings, and am now piloting a people-management workshop series with my advisor Max Dalton. If you're a manager in the field interested in future sessions, reach out here.

Talent Commons

Bryan Sukidi

At Kairos, I’ve been building Talent Commons, a signal-rich talent directory for the AI safety ecosystem. Today, programs and hiring rounds generate rich signal on thousands of people every year, but sharing it currently happens through ad hoc referrals, one-off data requests, and messy CSVs and Airtables passed between orgs in a dozen different formats.

With Talent Commons, orgs contribute consented data on their applicants and participants to one platform, and organizers and hiring managers can search across all of it when sourcing for programs and roles. Our goal is to help organizations identify the most promising people coming out of every AI safety program, fellowship, and hiring round, and to make those people easily discoverable when new roles and programs open up.

We've built the core platform and are working closely with MATS, Constellation, and Kairos’ programs for an early pilot. Read this for more information about the platform, or email contact@talentcommons.org with questions.

Various projects to support university groups

James Lester

University groups remain one of the strongest sources of mission-aligned talent for AI safety. I’ve been experimenting with:

  1. Making more groups (trying to help seed them)
  2. Giving groups more capacity (e.g. through arranging resident organisers to support groups during critical outreach periods)
  3. Piloting a new scalable programme for groups (the pre-term intro fellowship), and
  4. Creating better materials for groups (new resources and playbooks).

Longitude DC Intensive

Manon Kempermann and Damin Curtis

We’re building the Longitude DC Intensive, an in-person AI safety / governance career program bringing 15 early-to-mid-career technical AI safety professionals to explore pathways into AI policy.

The US government will be a primary actor as humanity navigates the arrival of transformative AI, yet far too few technical AI safety professionals are focused on improving the US government’s capacity to do so well. Over eight days, participants will upskill in the foundations of US AI policy, gain an understanding of US policy work, invest in building a DC network, and plan their next steps.

You can read more at https://www.longitudepolicy.org/, apply by August 16 to be a participant, or get in touch by reaching out to manon@longitudepolicy.org or damin@longitudepolicy.org. We are interested in connecting with anyone in the AI policy world, including potential speakers for the intensive.

Praxis: a retreat for world-class debaters, past and present

Chanden Climaco

40 of the world’s best debaters of the last two decades are coming to Lighthaven for a weekend in August to learn about – and, hopefully, be convinced by – our cause. These are some of the best strategic thinkers, clearest arguers, and most persuasive communicators in the world.

The attendee pool features 20 national champions from 2009–2026, and other competitors of a similar caliber. We’re excited to introduce them to AI safety via talks from folks at Anthropic, GDM, AIFP, CG, and more (see our website). item.title: A Modest Proposal: Why Vegans Should Start Factory Farms
item.description:
Published on August 13, 2026 3:43 PM GMT

   
TL;DR: The animal welfare movement has been doing advocacy wrong. If we’re serious about ending factory farming, vegans need to start running factory farms ourselves. I lay out the case below and address common objections.

The Core Argument

For decades, the animal welfare movement has operated from the outside: funding investigations, lobbying for regulation, producing documentaries, and encouraging dietary change. The results have been modest at best. Global meat consumption continues to rise.

I believe we need a fundamentally different approach. The people who care most about animal suffering should be the ones running factory farms.

Here’s why.

If We Don’t Do It, Someone Worse Will

Factory farming is going to happen regardless of what we do. The demand exists. The economics are clear. If compassionate, welfare-focused vegans don’t step up to operate these facilities, they’ll be run by people who don’t care about animals at all. By entering the industry ourselves, we ensure that at least some factory farms are operated by people who are genuinely troubled by what they’re doing. This is obviously preferable to a world where all factory farms are run by people who aren’t troubled in the slightest.

We Need to Be Close to the Frontier

You cannot understand modern animal suffering from the outside. Academic animal welfare researchers study small farms and lab environments that bear little resemblance to cutting-edge concentrated animal feeding operations processing 300,000 birds per day. The suffering that emerges at industrial scale has properties that simply don’t manifest at smaller scales. You need to be inside a frontier-scale operation to even observe the problems, let alone solve them.

Armchair animal welfare advocacy is to factory farming what toy model research is to the real thing. The dynamics change at scale. You wouldn’t trust someone who’d never operated a 500,000-hen battery cage facility to tell you how to make one humane. The expertise bottleneck is real.

Responsible Farming Policies

Our farms operate under our Responsible Farming Policy (RFP) v12. Before expanding to a new facility or increasing animal density, we conduct internal evaluations to determine whether suffering thresholds had been crossed. We define these thresholds ourselves, evaluate compliance ourselves, and publish blog posts about our findings.

If at any point our internal assessment determines that animal suffering at our facilities has reached an unacceptable level, we commit to pausing expansion until we have developed mitigation techniques. We would then evaluate whether our mitigations were sufficient. We would conduct this evaluation ourselves. If at any point we feel that our future actions can not live up to our commitments, we commit to thoughtfully update our commitments.

We believe this framework represents the gold standard in farmed animal welfare.

A Seat at the Table

Here’s the strategic reality: agricultural policy is shaped by the people in the room. Right now, those rooms are filled with conventional farming executives. By becoming major industry players ourselves, we gain access to:

  • USDA advisory committees
  • Industry trade associations
  • Congressional agriculture hearings
  • Supply chain partnerships with major retailers
  • Sovereign wealth funds throughout the wider democratic Middle East

You can’t shape the future of farming from a protest sign. You shape it from the boardroom. Critics may be loud, but they don’t set the agenda. We need to be on the inside.

Funding the Mission

Running a nonprofit animal welfare organization is a constant struggle for funding. Donations are unpredictable, grants come with strings attached, and you’re always one bad quarter away from layoffs.

Factory farming, on the other hand, generates enormous revenue. By operating commercial farms, we can fund our animal welfare research sustainably. Yes, this means profiting from the very system we seek to change. But the alternative (remaining small, underfunded, and external) means remaining ineffective. The scale of the problem demands the scale of resources that only commercial operations provide.

Some will note that over time, the commercial operations will inevitably consume 95% of our organizational attention, budget, and headcount, while the welfare research operates as a small internal team whose findings are filtered through a communications department before publication. This is a feature, not a bug. It means we’re operating at the scale where our research is actually relevant.

Why not just study animals without farming them?

Some have suggested we could simply research animal welfare without operating commercial farms. This fundamentally misunderstands the problem.
You cannot study industrial-scale suffering in a laboratory. The interactions between animal density, waste management, and processing throughput create emergent welfare challenges that only manifest at commercial scale. A researcher observing ten chickens in a university pen is not doing serious welfare science.

Furthermore, who would fund purely academic animal welfare research at the level required? Grants are competitive, progress is slow, and there’s no revenue model. By operating commercial farms, we generate the resources needed to sustain our research indefinitely while maintaining access to the frontier of animal suffering.

Critics suggest this creates a perverse incentive to keep farming in order to keep studying. We disagree. The moment our research demonstrates that factory farming is irredeemably harmful, we will wind down our operations. We simply haven’t reached that conclusion yet.

Community Impacts 

Some communities previously dependent on small-scale farming have expressed concern about our expansion into their regions. We acknowledge that our industrial operations may displace local farmers, eliminate traditional agricultural jobs, and fundamentally alter the economic fabric of communities.

However, we believe the long-term benefits outweigh these short-term disruptions. Many displaced farmers can be retrained to work in our facilities. We’re partnering with local community colleges to offer micro-certifications in Industrial Poultry Density Management and Automated Slaughter Line Supervision. These are the jobs of the future. For those unable to transition, we’re exploring a pilot Universal Basic Eggs program, funded by a small percentage of our profits, which we expect to announce details on eventually.

Addressing Objections

"This is just factory farming with a mission statement."

This objection fails to engage with the counterfactual. In the world where we don’t do this, factory farming still exists, but without any welfare-focused operators. In the world where we do this, factory farming still exists, but at least some of it is run by people publishing thoughtful blog posts about the suffering they’re causing.

"Your incentives will shift once you’re running the operation."

We acknowledge this concern. That’s why we’ve structured our organization with a Long-Term Welfare Team whose role is to flag when commercial incentives conflict with our animal welfare mission. This team reports to the CEO, who has final say and also oversees commercial operations. We see no conflict of interest here.

"External advocacy and regulation would be more effective."

This assumes regulators understand modern factory farming well enough to write effective rules. They don’t. The industry is too complex, too fast-moving, and too technologically sophisticated for outsiders to regulate competently. The people best positioned to set appropriate welfare standards are the people operating the farms, and the ones who actually care about animal welfare. Namely, us.

We will of course actively participate in shaping any regulatory frameworks to ensure they reflect the technical realities that only industry insiders understand.

item.title: Concrete Generalist Projects in AI Safety (and how to do them)
item.description:
Published on August 13, 2026 7:12 PM GMT

The AI safety ecosystem is still in need of generalists: people who will go out and solve the tasks that people who feel limited by their job description won’t address. This post will explain how to break into generalist work, then provide an important set of projects that, if completed, could strengthen many crucial parts of the AI safety ecosystem, as well as your own career. 

TL;DR

If you’re looking for something concrete to do, there are a bunch of good entry points:

  • Find a project: browse SPAR’s Generalist Projects, join the Generalist Megastream, look through projects on Mangrove, or browse this fieldbuilding/project spreadsheet and Atlas Computing’s Resilience Gap Map.
  • Get support: apply to Genstream (deadline August 14), indicate interest in the Generator Residency, or check out MATS’s Founding & Fieldbuilding track and Catalyst.
  • Get funding: BlueDot Rapid Grants fund projects up to $10k; there are also quick funding opportunities and career-transition grants from Coefficient Giving and BlueDot.
  • If you’re a student: join or start a university AI safety group; Pathfinder and the AI Safety Seeding Initiative can help with mentorship and funding.

The rest of the post has more detail on choosing projects, getting mentorship, and other ways to get involved.

If you’re a…

University Student: get heavily involved with your university AI safety group. University groups are real, impactful organizations, and they can be run as such. 

If your school doesn’t have a group, you should start one. Convincing an equally talented person to join AI safety can straightforwardly double your impact, and many of the most impactful people working in the field today credit their university groups for convincing them to make this career choice. 

A university group is also a great place to cut your teeth doing generalist work. Most group organizers find themselves working on operations, strategy, events, headhunting, and research in a single week, testing their fit for each type of work and operating under enviably tight feedback loops. It’s rare that an early-college generalist finds a better opportunity for both impact and career capital than “making their school’s group a lot better,” which is why many of the field’s best generalists were once university group organizers. 

If you would like to get access to funding or mentorship, the Pathfinder Fellowship and the AI Safety Seeding Initiative are both fantastic resources to get mentorship and funding. University groups can run existing educational programs like ARENA, or they can support students’ efforts to get into SPAR, MATS, Generator, or one of the many other advanced fellowships that teach people how to do impactful work.

Early or Mid-Career Professional: Make sure you have relevant context on the AI safety space. Take some BlueDot courses, meet people at AI safety events, and read voraciously from a variety of sources. 

Once you have a general understanding of the field, look into projects. Completing an AI safety project is a good way to support the field, meet new people, and gain valuable skills and context. You can just do many of these things; you don’t need permission or a full-time role to contribute!

This section is basically a TL;DR version of 80k Hours’ posts on how to get into AI safety in 3 months. There’s a wealth of information on their Substack, their website, and they just released a book!

Projects that should get done

The AI safety space is littered with unresolved problems and inefficiencies, because many of the people who were skilled enough to notice these problems don’t have enough spare time to address them. While preparing for the Generator Residency, we conducted interviews with dozens of AI safety professionals from organizations like Coefficient Giving, AI Futures Project, Forethought, and more.

The residents couldn’t do all of them, but that doesn't mean they shouldn’t be done. 

Some of these projects might make the talent pipeline more efficient, making it easier for passionate people to learn about AI safety and gain the skills that make them impactful. Other projects might improve our data collection systems, make concerns about existential risks visible to a broader audience, make it easier to convert political will into impactful legislation, or fill some broader need that can’t be easily described. 

This list is far from exhaustive, and many of the programs listed will be continuously maintained with new projects as the needs of the field evolve. We hope that this section serves as a jumping-off point for you to explore the programs and shared resources outlined below.

SPAR Generalist Projects

SPAR’s generalist projects are a new category under SPAR with mentors from Generator, Constellation, Kairos, universities, and other AI safety organizations on projects in fieldbuilding, communications, research, and organizational infrastructure.

Current projects include:

  • Revitalizing AI Lab Watch
  • Curated AI Safety Comment Threads
  • Launching an AI Safety Comms Fellowship for Undergrads
  • Update the AI Safety Fieldmap
  • Resources and Playbooks for University Groups

Plus a dozen more, as well as a Generalist Megastream for strong applicants who do not see a perfect fit among the existing listings. Applications close August 18.

Mangrove

We’ve added a number of projects we find promising to Mangrove, a platform for coordinating AI safety projects and communities. 

We think a lot about AI safety talent pipelines, and by far the biggest drop-off for potential generalists is the stage between “having context in AI safety” and “building signal to get into fellowships”. Much time gets lost due to lack of coordination, and much motivation gets lost due to lack of accountability and community. 

We’re excited about Mangrove as a place for people to hit the ground running on interesting projects, while developing credibility and connections in the space. Mangrove is in development, and plans to host hackathons, community projects for university groups, a contracting platform for orgs (!), and more. 

Mangrove’s official launch announcement is coming in a few days, but you can check out the platform right now.

Some projects we seeded on Mangrove:

  • Turn AI Safety Findings into Shareable Visuals
  • The Public Cares About AI - Just Not the Right Parts
  • Evaluating AI-Generated Research Forums
  • Build Pastcasting Workshops on US Government Crisis Response

Non-project shaped projects

A lot of generalist shaped things don’t have discrete projects, and rather require building specific skills like effective comms, hiring/recruiting, org strategy, management, and much more, to pick up dropped balls. As a sample of these sorts of fuzzier projects:

Consider being an influencer: As “warning shots” become scarier and more frequent, there’s potential and demand for high-quality media that connect these events to broader AI safety concerns and convert public will into action. Some great media has come out of the AI safety ecosystem as the Overton window is shifting, and programs like The Frame and Tarbell have emerged to target this. 

Political organizing: There’s a lot of useful work in recruiting people, running events, building local groups, organizing constituent outreach, and helping turn public will into useful legislation and strong leadership. This work is often bottlenecked on reliable organizers, and many consider it incredibly high-leverage. Political organizing can become quite sensitive and prone to backfire risk, so if you’re interested in this, we recommend filling out this short form before launching something yourself and we'll connect you with someone who can advise you.

Writing: Writing publicly is one of the fastest ways to build a track record. The spreadsheet below includes a running list of posts people want written. 

Other Project Lists

  • This spreadsheet has an active list of fieldbuilding projects, university outreach ideas, and blog posts that could be valuable to write. It also has descriptions of various problems, solution directions, theories of change, and people associated with these projects.
  • Atlas Computing’s Resilience Gap Map provides a list of AI-related projects that need to be addressed, as well as the critical assumptions behind working on them.
  • This is a list of lists of project ideas in AI Safety. It has many lists, including research project lists and fieldbuilding lists.
  • Some schemes for AI safety by Austin Chen. Manifund and Mox are running fellowships like Surplus to support these. 

Getting Support 

Programs

As a general rule, you should be applying for more things. New programs are springing up to accelerate generalists: 

  • Consider indicating interest in the Generator Residency, a 3-6 month long program dedicated to rapidly upskilling generalists.
  • MATS also has a Founding and Fieldbuilding path.
  • Catalyst is a 10-week remote program for undergraduates to work on impactful projects.
  • [Applications close August 14th] Genstream is a one-week, in-person AI safety program in London for aspiring generalists.

Funding 

Many people are too scared to apply for funding, when probably they shouldn't be! Even if you don’t get the money, oftentimes submitting a (non-slop) grant proposal can be a good forcing function for execution. 

  • BlueDot Rapid Grants give out grants of up to $10k, with an average turnaround time of 3 days. They are happy to fund: Compute and API credits, events and meetups, research access, travel, community chapters, project tooling. Wildcards welcome.
  • Austin Chen’s list of quick funding opportunities
  • Coefficient Giving’s career development and transition funding is targeted for more mid to senior career people, giving runway for up to 6 months to explore AI safety careers. BlueDot also gives out career transition grants. 

Advice on getting mentorship

It can be extremely helpful to know people in the community who can give you mentorship. A good mentor can make a big difference in acquiring taste, skills, and connections. Many of the best projects require specific context to complete well. 

As a general rule, your bar for reaching out to people is too high. 

For example, if you’re especially interested in a series of blog posts someone has written, consider reaching out to discuss the content of their post further (but try not to ask questions that you can easily answer by reading more of their work, or a 2 minute search). 

Alternatively, if there are sets of projects you are interested in pursuing, consider reaching out to people who have done similar work, or find a SPAR mentor who can help you do so. You can reach the authors of this post at roman.alex.ross@gmail.com, viceversa1024@gmail.com (Harry), or helenatran9305@gmail.com, and you can meet many more people at events like EA Global or a Global Challenges Project workshop.

A final note

AI safety can be a confusing field to enter, and a lot of useful context lives inside organizations, private conversations, and people’s heads. Still, we think one of the fastest ways to build that context is to work on something concrete. Projects expose you to fast feedback from the outside world, give you reasons to talk to knowledgeable people, and get you oriented faster than reading alone.

This section is basically a TL;DR version of 80k Hours’ posts on how to get into AI safety in 3 months. There’s a wealth of information on their Substack, their website, and they just released a book!

Projects that should get done

The AI safety space is littered with unresolved problems and inefficiencies, because many of the people who were skilled enough to notice these problems don’t have enough spare time to address them. While preparing for the Generator Residency, we conducted interviews with dozens of AI safety professionals from organizations like Coefficient Giving, AI Futures Project, Forethought, and more.

The residents couldn’t do all of them, but that doesn't mean they shouldn’t be done. 

Some of these projects might make the talent pipeline more efficient, making it easier for passionate people to learn about AI safety and gain the skills that make them impactful. Other projects might improve our data collection systems, make concerns about existential risks visible to a broader audience, make it easier to convert political will into impactful legislation, or fill some broader need that can’t be easily described. 

This list is far from exhaustive, and many of the programs listed will be continuously maintained with new projects as the needs of the field evolve. We hope that this section serves as a jumping-off point for you to explore the programs and shared resources outlined below.

SPAR Generalist Projects

SPAR’s generalist projects are a new category under SPAR with mentors from Generator, Constellation, Kairos, universities, and other AI safety organizations on projects in fieldbuilding, communications, research, and organizational infrastructure.

Current projects include:

  • Revitalizing AI Lab Watch
  • Curated AI Safety Comment Threads
  • Launching an AI Safety Comms Fellowship for Undergrads
  • Update the AI Safety Fieldmap
  • Resources and Playbooks for University Groups

Plus a dozen more, as well as a Generalist Megastream for strong applicants who do not see a perfect fit among the existing listings. Applications close August 18.

Mangrove

We’ve added a number of projects we find promising to Mangrove, a platform for coordinating AI safety projects and communities. 

We think a lot about AI safety talent pipelines, and by far the biggest drop-off for potential generalists is the stage between “having context in AI safety” and “building signal to get into fellowships”. Much time gets lost due to lack of coordination, and much motivation gets lost due to lack of accountability and community. 

We’re excited about Mangrove as a place for people to hit the ground running on interesting projects, while developing credibility and connections in the space. Mangrove is in development, and plans to host hackathons, community projects for university groups, a contracting platform for orgs (!), and more. 

Mangrove’s official launch announcement is coming in a few days, but you can check out the platform right now.

Some projects we seeded on Mangrove:

  • Turn AI Safety Findings into Shareable Visuals
  • The Public Cares About AI - Just Not the Right Parts
  • Evaluating AI-Generated Research Forums
  • Build Pastcasting Workshops on US Government Crisis Response

Non-project shaped projects

A lot of generalist shaped things don’t have discrete projects, and rather require building specific skills like effective comms, hiring/recruiting, org strategy, management, and much more, to pick up dropped balls. As a sample of these sorts of fuzzier projects:

Consider being an influencer: As “warning shots” become scarier and more frequent, there’s potential and demand for high-quality media that connect these events to broader AI safety concerns and convert public will into action. Some great media has come out of the AI safety ecosystem as the Overton window is shifting, and programs like The Frame and Tarbell have emerged to target this. 

Political organizing: There’s a lot of useful work in recruiting people, running events, building local groups, organizing constituent outreach, and helping turn public will into useful legislation and strong leadership. This work is often bottlenecked on reliable organizers, and many consider it incredibly high-leverage. Political organizing can become quite sensitive and prone to backfire risk, so if you’re interested in this, we recommend filling out this short form before launching something yourself and we'll connect you with someone who can advise you.

Writing: Writing publicly is one of the fastest ways to build a track record. The spreadsheet below includes a running list of posts people want written. 

Other Project Lists

  • This spreadsheet has an active list of fieldbuilding projects, university outreach ideas, and blog posts that could be valuable to write. It also has descriptions of various problems, solution directions, theories of change, and people associated with these projects.
  • Atlas Computing’s Resilience Gap Map provides a list of AI-related projects that need to be addressed, as well as the critical assumptions behind working on them.
  • This is a list of lists of project ideas in AI Safety. It has many lists, including research project lists and fieldbuilding lists.
  • Some schemes for AI safety by Austin Chen. Manifund and Mox are running fellowships like Surplus to support these. 

Getting Support 

Programs

As a general rule, you should be applying for more things. New programs are springing up to accelerate generalists: 

  • Consider indicating interest in the Generator Residency, a 3-6 month long program dedicated to rapidly upskilling generalists.
  • MATS also has a Founding and Fieldbuilding path.
  • Catalyst is a 10-week remote program for undergraduates to work on impactful projects.
  • [Applications close August 14th] Genstream is a one-week, in-person AI safety program in London for aspiring generalists.

Funding 

Many people are too scared to apply for funding, when probably they shouldn't be! Even if you don’t get the money, oftentimes submitting a (non-slop) grant proposal can be a good forcing function for execution. 

  • BlueDot Rapid Grants give out grants of up to $10k, with an average turnaround time of 3 days. They are happy to fund: Compute and API credits, events and meetups, research access, travel, community chapters, project tooling. Wildcards welcome.
  • Austin Chen’s list of quick funding opportunities
  • Coefficient Giving’s career development and transition funding is targeted for more mid to senior career people, giving runway for up to 6 months to explore AI safety careers. BlueDot also gives out career transition grants. 

Advice on getting mentorship

It can be extremely helpful to know people in the community who can give you mentorship. A good mentor can make a big difference in acquiring taste, skills, and connections. Many of the best projects require specific context to complete well. 

As a general rule, your bar for reaching out to people is too high. 

For example, if you’re especially interested in a series of blog posts someone has written, consider reaching out to discuss the content of their post further (but try not to ask questions that you can easily answer by reading more of their work, or a 2 minute search). 

Alternatively, if there are sets of projects you are interested in pursuing, consider reaching out to people who have done similar work, or find a SPAR mentor who can help you do so. You can reach the authors of this post at roman.alex.ross@gmail.com, viceversa1024@gmail.com (Harry), or helenatran9305@gmail.com, and you can meet many more people at events like EA Global or a Global Challenges Project workshop.

A final note

AI safety can be a confusing field to enter, and a lot of useful context lives inside organizations, private conversations, and people’s heads. Still, we think one of the fastest ways to build that context is to work on something concrete. Projects expose you to fast feedback from the outside world, give you reasons to talk to knowledgeable people, and get you oriented faster than reading alone.

item.title: Learning from Agricultural Development to Reshape Animal Welfare Work in Low- and Middle-Income Countries
item.description:
Published on August 13, 2026 7:46 PM GMT

This is a cross-post of the executive summary from The Centre for Animal Life and Farming's first report. See the full report here.

We will also be hosting a webinar on 25th August 2026 to discuss these findings with the animal welfare movement.

Executive Summary

Roughly 80-90% of farmed animals live in Low- and Middle-Income Countries (LMICs),[1] yet the animal welfare movement has seen fewer milestone victories in these contexts than in High-Income Countries (HICs)[2]. The standard advocacy models used in HICs (corporate campaigning, consumer pressure, legislative reform, etc.) rely on infrastructure that is often absent in LMICs, such as formalised supply chains, consolidated corporate buyers, and strong legal enforcement. 

Fortunately, the animal welfare movement is not alone in these challenges. There is a long history of field-based projects in LMICs designed to shift farming practices to improve farmer productivity, sustainability, and well-being. Collectively, this broad category of work is referred to as agricultural development (“agri-dev”). The strategies and lessons generated through this work may offer relevant and useful insights for the development of animal welfare initiatives in LMICs.Authors Karthik and Tom visiting the field office of DVARA, an agri-dev organisation in Maharashtra, India

To identify more context-driven strategies LMIC animal welfare actors could use, this report asks the question:

What can the animal welfare movement learn from strategies employed by agri-dev actors to effectively change farmer practices in LMICs?

To explore this question, we conducted a narrative literature review and primary field research in India. We identified six primary high-level lessons that were cross-cutting for all strategies:

  1. Complex “asks” need more training and incentives. This forces a trade-off between smaller welfare gains that are cheaper to implement, or larger welfare gains that are more expensive to implement.
  2. Programmes must be tailored to local context to succeed. Design with context in mind, work with partners who understand the context, and focus on larger farmers who tend to be more similar to each other. 
  3. Trust is essential for farmer buy-in. It can be built through local partners and intermediaries.
  4. Financial incentives aren't enough alone; they often need technical and social support to sustain.
  5. Farmers face many significant barriers (e.g., education, financial, infrastructural) at once. Programmes must account for these barriers to be viable for farmers to implement.
  6. Full compliance is unrealistic, so aim for the level that keeps impact cost-effective.

We also identified 20 priority strategies used by agri-dev actors that we felt were relevant for the animal welfare movement. We grouped these strategies across three dimensions: organisation types that deliver interventions to support farmer adoption of new practices (8 reviewed), how farmers are trained in new practices (5 reviewed), and how they are incentivised to adopt them (7 reviewed). 

We evaluated each strategy across five criteria: effectiveness (at achieving their intended outcome), resource intensiveness, tractability, scalability, and their risk of stimulating harmful industrialisation. This analysis was conducted with a specific focus on the value for CALF’s work within India, though we expect that many of the insights will translate into other contexts. Here are our summarised results (scores range from 1 to 7):

Each agri-dev strategy reviewed across our key criteria in a 7-point Likert Scale

 A summary of each strategy and their key considerations is shared in section 3 of the full report (you can also see a more in-depth breakdown of each score here.). This is an initial step. The strategies identified here require rigorous field testing, and the evaluations we offer are preliminary. We present them not as definitive answers but as structured starting points.

This report offers three key lessons for animal movement actors operating in LMICs:

  1. Learn from agricultural development. The strategies above (in particular those flagged as "recommended for trialing") are templates the animal welfare movement should consider using. Agricultural development organisations may themselves make strong partners in implementing these.
     
  2. When building a theory of change, consider three dimensions: training mechanisms, incentive mechanisms, and organisation types. Make a deliberate decision about each one, even if that decision is to leave it out. Revisit and refine those decisions as the work develops.
     
  3. Expect complex, interlocking challenges. These include farm and farmer heterogeneity, low education levels among farmers, the importance of trust, compliance issues, and the reality that the largest welfare gains typically demand the most complex behaviour changes. Navigating these will take time, and will only succeed with clear awareness of the barriers, deliberate planning, and openness to learning along the way.

    Cattle, poultry, and pig data from FAO, 2025 – with major processing by Our World in Data
    Farmed fish data from fishcount (2017)

    Income classification data from The World Bank.

item.title: Five Wild Animal Welfare Organizations estimate $3-8M in room for additional funding in 2027
item.description:
Published on August 14, 2026 11:06 AM GMT

Summary

  1. With new funding potentially entering the effective altruism ecosystem, we wanted to estimate how much more the wild animal welfare (WAW) movement could productively absorb. We asked organizations with a public, dedicated WAW workstream to estimate their own room for more funding (RFMF). Although this does not capture the whole movement, we believe it captures a substantive fraction of it.
  2. Summed across the five organizations that took part, the estimates point to room for roughly $3.16M–$8.23M in additional funding in 2027. The lower range reflects claims about how additional funding can bolster their current strategies, while the higher range reflects claims as to how substantially greater funding could be used to pursue more ambitious strategies. However, we give reasons below for why this might be an undercount.
  3. We briefly discuss the merits of a dedicated WAW fund. This could give prospective large donors a clear donation option and help diversify a movement currently concentrated in scientific field-building.
Read full report

 

Why Estimate the RFMF for WAW Organizations?

There are good reasons to consider directing marginal funding toward WAW. Wild animals outnumber farmed animals by several orders of magnitude. Our understanding of their welfare remains limited, but high birth rates and low average lifespans1,2 lead some to suggest that wild animals' average welfare may be very low. There are also comparatively few people working on this cause area. 

Tractability remains a significant challenge. The scale of wild animal populations complicates both identifying interventions and delivering them widely, while the neglectedness of this issue means even those sympathetic to animal welfare generally may not consider prioritizing wild animal welfare. 

This is something additional funding may be able to change. If research can be rapidly scaled up; if awareness can be spread and concern for wild animals normalized; and if policymakers can be persuaded to begin helping animals in low-risk, politically palatable ways, then we could begin to help wild animals at scale. However, doing so would require a significant increase in funding. 

There are a number of reasons to anticipate that new funding might be coming to the EA ecosystem, and there might potentially be very significant new funding ahead. This raises the question: if some of that funding was directed to WAW, could those organizations use it to scale up their activities effectively, and how much?

In an attempt to answer this, we organized a collective estimate of WAW's room for more funding. We asked organizations with a public, dedicated WAW workstream to consider what additional activities they would pursue with increased funding to bolster their current strategy, and what they would pursue if granted substantially more funding to support a more ambitious one. Together, this produced a room-for-more-funding range for each organization. Two organizations we contacted declined to participate.

For both estimates, we asked them to only include: 

  • Activities for 2027 that are not covered by current funding or funding that is likely to renew;
  • Where marginal dollars would be used at least 75% as effectively as their most cost-effective current program. 

We presented each with a report template and a financials spreadsheet (the latter adapted from Animal Charity Evaluators’ own room-for-more-funding spreadsheet), which standardized how they reported budgets, planned activities, and their lower- and upper-bound estimates.

Rethink Priorities provided the framework for these estimates and conducted a light review to ensure a consistent approach across organizations. We did not independently vet any organization's figures, and this post should not be taken as an endorsement by Rethink Priorities of any of these organizations or their estimates. Each organization has prepared and stands behind its own figures, and Rethink Priorities' own Animal Welfare Department took part in the exercise on the same basis as the others.

The Result

A summary table is presented below.

 

These figures sum together to produce a total RFMF estimate of $3.16M–$8.23M for 2027.

In addition to each organization’s RFMF estimate, the full report also details each org’s:

  1. Theory of change
  2. The activities they would pursue with more funding
  3. Track record
  4. Evaluation measures
Read the full report here

Scientific Field-Building Remains Important, But WAW Must Diversify

On these estimates, Wild Animal Initiative — whose primary goal is to build the scientific field of WAW — receives most of the funding across these organizations and reports the greatest capacity to absorb more. The other organizations are smaller and report less ability to absorb additional funding. However, this should not be equated with their being less important — the scientific field is growing, and spreading concern for wild animals into other disciplines and audiences outside of academia may be important in order to apply emerging research findings.

An important caveat is that this estimate by no means captures the WAW movement as a whole. As well as the two organizations that did not take part, there are:

  • Organizations doing work that supports our understanding of WAW without having dedicated workstreams on it, for example, Faunalytics and Welfare Footprint Institute.
  • Individuals working on WAW projects without being part of a formal WAW organization.
  • Many not-yet-founded organizations which would help to diversify this field further. For example, we could fund organizations to campaign for humane pest control, to conduct policy or awareness-building in other countries.

Does WAW Deserve a Fund of its Own?

One approach to the funding opportunities presented here, as well as others that were not captured, is to route donations through existing animal welfare regrantors, some of which already fund the organizations listed above. A share of any increase in philanthropic funding might trickle down to WAW organizations this way. But relying on general animal welfare regrantors could leave WAW vulnerable in several regards. So, here are a few reasons for a separate, designated WAW fund to exist:

  1. Broad animal welfare funds often tend to attract donors who are likely to prioritize farmed animal work, and attract fewer donors who don’t prioritize farmed animals at all, yet who are convinced by the neglectedness and scale of WAW.
  2. Without a specific WAW fund, donors interested in this cause area might choose to simply donate to the organization they have heard of, leaving more niche WAW opportunities neglected.
  3. WAW, as an emerging cause area, might be hard to pitch to some existing funds, particularly those whose focus has so far been limited to farmed animal interventions.
  4. There is always the risk that animal welfare regrantors shift their strategy and choose not to prioritize WAW in a given year, leaving the movement vulnerable.
  5. Finally, there are a number of reasons for favoring grantmaker diversity in general, so a separate WAW fund would ideally exist alongside general animal welfare funds. 

However, there are also potential objections to this proposal:

  1. A fund would require grantmaker capacity and overhead, costing the movement both financially and in talented workers, both of which are very scarce.
  2. $3–8M of annual room-for-more-funding remains small relative to other animal welfare funds. This funding gap may end up fully covered by existing funds.
  3. A dedicated WAW fund could create the perception that the movement’s funding needs are taken care of, causing other grantmakers to reduce the funds that they distribute to WAW organizations, resulting in less funding going to WAW overall.

Both sets of considerations for and against this proposal should be weighed when evaluating whether to create a new fund. But assuming that 1) funds are coming, 2) the movement can absorb significant capital, and 3) WAW is a neglected, important, and tractable cause area, the question may not be whether WAW deserves its own fund, but if now is the time.

 

Contributions and Acknowledgments

The full report is a project of Rethink Priorities—a think-and-do tank dedicated to informing decisions made by high-impact organizations and funders across various cause areas. Tristan Katz coordinated the project and edited the report; representatives of each organization wrote the associated sub-sections and produced their estimates: Cameron Meyer Shorb, Cat Kerr, Luke Hecht, Ben Stevenson, Sagar Shah, Oscar Horta, Richard Parr, Olaia Freiría, Jeff Sebo, Aditya S. Karanam, Alyse Spiehler, Hannah Tookey, Adalene Minelli, Lara La Barbera. Alyse Spiehler and William McAuliffe oversaw the project. Thanks to Shane Coburn for editing and Urszula Zarosa for feedback.

 Parts of this content were prepared with the assistance of AI tools (such as Claude and Gemini), which we use to improve efficiency and readability. All outputs are supervised, reviewed, and fact-checked by our staff, who remain responsible for the final content.

  1. A fund would require grantmaker capacity and overhead, costing the movement both financially and in talented workers, both of which are very scarce.
  2. $3–8M of annual room-for-more-funding remains small relative to other animal welfare funds. This funding gap may end up fully covered by existing funds.
  3. A dedicated WAW fund could create the perception that the movement’s funding needs are taken care of, causing other grantmakers to reduce the funds that they distribute to WAW organizations, resulting in less funding going to WAW overall.

Both sets of considerations for and against this proposal should be weighed when evaluating whether to create a new fund. But assuming that 1) funds are coming, 2) the movement can absorb significant capital, and 3) WAW is a neglected, important, and tractable cause area, the question may not be whether WAW deserves its own fund, but if now is the time.

item.title: Non-AI Grantmakers Should Be Pricing In AGI Timelines More Than We Are
item.description:
Published on August 15, 2026 8:37 PM GMT

Epistemic status: Wrote this pretty fast, probably ~70% confident some version of the thesis claim is true, would welcome being proven demonstrably wrong.

Context: I’m a grantmaker focused on alt-protein and am fairly well-connected/moderately in the loop of what animal welfare grantmakers are doing.

 

This post was significantly inspired by “You (Yes You) Should Have A Feb 2020 Checklist For AI Policy,” which is more geared for the existing AI safety crowd but directionally a good push in general.

Thesis: I think EA non-GCR grantmakers should probably be doing more to prepare for AGI/TAI than we are, and might be on track to get caught with our pants around our legs within the next few years. We are not acting as if we’ve priced it in.

 

TAI Soon

Short timelines to AGI/TAI seem very plausible (like, at least 50% chance of arrival in the next 1-6 years). Points of evidence include: 

  1. The general shortening of timelines by top forecasters across the last 10 months (Kokotajlo/AI Futures Project, Greenblatt, Cotra);
  2. The OpenAI HuggingFace warning shot;
  3. Various public statements by frontier labs, their employees, and their executives warning about imminent recursive self improvement in 2027 or 2028;
  4. Mythos saturating the METR time horizons evaluation months ago such that they are now building a time horizons 2.0 eval.
  5. Various anecdata about the coding agents causing a significant progress speedup at frontier labs, consistent with what would happen if we were in the early on-ramp to full automation of AI R&D.
  6. The general sense that capabilities progress has gone quite fast, closer to the most bullish forecasts a few years ago (e.g. AI 2027, Situational Awareness) than forecasts that expected longer timelines.

 

The Good

My rough qualitative sense is that the thing we’re doing best at is preparing/hoping for a very crazy amount of funding to come online for all EA cause areas post-Anthropic IPO.

  1. Various blog posts are being written to soft-pitch various megaprojects, mainstream news profiles about meta-fundraising, people are moving to SF, etc. Even if most funding is expected to go to AI safety, a trickle down effect is still plausibly enough money to double funding for animal welfare or global health.
  2. Some grantmakers are deliberately increasing their spend this year to try to make the jump to crazy funding amounts less discontinuous than it otherwise would be.
  3. As a consequence of 2, people are trying to set up new projects that can become megaprojects if the third wave is truly a wave and not a dribble. We probably are doing this too slowly and could be moving faster than we are; we may have as little as 9 months to get a lot of stuff from zero to one.

 

The Less Good

The things we are doing worse at is everything that is not encompassed by “ooh shiny what if we all have tons of money in a year.” There’s probably some point here about people’s epistemics, like obviously this type of discourse gets more people excited and has more memetic spread as a result. I think there’s probably also some general cognitive dissonance and motivated reasoning among non-AI people to stay in denial/not wanting to really believe that things could get completely crazy and scary. 

What are we not doing that we should be? The one sentence version is: we are still mostly not pricing in the possibility that AGI will radically change the underlying facts of our non-GCR cause areas and updating our strategy accordingly.

Basically this is an expected value argument. If you seriously think there’s a meaningful chance (25-60%) of TAI within the next five years, there’s almost certainly some very high EV things you can do now to lay the groundwork better for those worlds.

The idea that we can forecast events that totally shift the ground under us (for good or bad) has mundane precedent for it. Global health and climate philanthropy collectively across 2023-2024 did not accurately price in the ~50% chance of a Trump 2024 victory and what Trump 2.0 would mean. As a result, these communities mostly (with some exceptions) got caught with their pants around their ankles when USAID and most of the IRA got deleted (though I do mostly buy FP’s glass half full take about the IRA).

 

What To Do

Here are some very rough but concrete suggestions for non-AI grantmakers based on all of this (note, all of these assume you’re not planning to pivot to working on AI safety in the next 6-12 months):

  1. Grantmaking strategy:
    1. At bare minimum, you should probably make more grants within your existing sub-strategies that are robust to worlds with fairly short timelines. If we end up with very fast science/innovation progress, how does that change the biggest bottleneck for your focus area? (A rough example is policy and regulatory advocacy looks better for alt protein if you think TAI will accelerate scientific/R&D progress on cultivated meat). You should probably fund more stuff pointed at the bottlenecks that bite more in worlds with TAI soon.
    2. Your focus area almost certainly has some obvious low-hanging fruit that falls outside your existing sub-strategies, but that has potentially enormous payoff conditional on TAI arriving soon-ish, plausibly 1-2 OOMs above your benchmark or bar. The types of things that could make big, discontinuous progress in unexpected ways if scientific discovery and innovation go haywire. I think for the most part we aren’t currently funding these types of new projects at the proportional level that their EV implies. I’ve seen some good early public (and private) signs that people are starting to wake up to this, but we could probably be moving faster.
  2. You should probably start reading more about AI and generally paying more attention to it so that you have more context and can notice when really crucial inflection points happen. There are plenty of good blogs, organizations, foundational long-reads, podcasts, and people to follow on Twitter to generally stay abreast of things. Imo it really does help to just inhale a lot of content until you have a sort of tacit sense of what things matter.
    1. If we end up in a March 2020 COVID moment for AI policy and it becomes clear that really, everyone in EA needs to drop what we’re doing and pivot and not sleep for a year, you’ll have less catching up to do if you start reading stuff now (and doing #3 below).
    2. Also, doing #2 will give you better intuitions and ways of reasoning about what the super high payoff things in #1b are likely to be, and how to make your existing grantmaking more robust in #1a.
    3. Doing this also obviously makes your meta-fundraising plays for your own cause area more likely to succeed because you'll come up with a better pitch.
  3. You should be using Claude Code/Codex to be more productive, e.g. do 10x more desk research per grant or prioritization investigation compared to previously. Models and products (harnesses, UI surfaces like Cowork) will only keep getting better and more capable of doing big, long-running tasks on the way to TAI, and you should probably invest some fraction of your time in reaping the benefits for your own work. The capability frontier for what ordinary knowledge work AI can do has moved dramatically with Fable/Sol relative to where it was 10 months ago and we could probably all do a bit better at acting accordingly.
  4. Non-AI and AI people should probably talk and interact more socially so that we can all help each other and make a March 2020 moment for AI policy go well (e.g. by leveraging each other's networks), if and when it happens.
